newsitem.title: FRANCE: French, foreign carmakers hit by truckers' strike.
newsitem.headline: French, foreign carmakers hit by truckers' strike.

text.p: A 10-day-old truckers' strike has interrupted production at French car factories for more than a week and is now disrupting industries in neighbouring countries.
Renault SA said production was halted on Wednesday at the Douai plant, which produces the new Megane Scenic car. A spokeswoman said all the access roads to the plant were blocked.
Production was expected to stop this afternoon at Renault's Flins plant, which has run low on parts.
Its Sandouville plant, which produces Safrane and Laguna cars, was put on short-time working all day on Wednesday.
The PSA group's Peugeot and Citroen divisions said their plants were all running on Wednesday, but officials said the situation could deteriorate quickly.
"The situation grows increasingly difficult. Even truckers who are getting through to deliver parts are having trouble finding enough fuel" said a Citroen spokesman.

Last week Peugeot reduced shifts at its Sochaux and Poissy plants in France, at its Madrid plant and at its Ryton plant in Britain. Citroen brought forward short-time working previously scheduled at its Rennes plant for Friday to Monday.
Volkswagen AG said it may introduce short-time working at its Wolfburg plant in Germany because the supply of car parts had been disrupted by the French strike.
VW imports heating and air conditioning systems for its Golf and Polo models from plants in central France and it imports metal parts from Spain.
The German carmaker said its Brussels plant may be affected by the French strike and that it also had trouble delivering components to its Seat subsidiary in Spain.
Opel France, a subsidiary of General Motors Corp, said drivers were unable to make deliveries to some dealers.

It said dealers in southeastern France were the most cut off because of roadblocks and fuel shortages. "In certain cities, like Caen and Bordeaux, we're having difficulty making deliveries," said Opel sales director Bertrand Belsens.
A spokesman for Ford Motor Co said production at its components plants in Bordeaux and Charleville was not affected.
Fiat said the strike was slowing deliveries to dealers, particularly in western and southwestern France, and might dent the group's November car sales, a spokesman said.
One car analyst estimated the strike could cost the French car industry "hundreds of millions of francs".
"Because of just-in-time deliveries (of components to assembly plants), car companies do get hit very quickly," he said. "This is causing enormous disruption."

Shares in Renault and in the Peugeot group have not been hit hard by the truckers' strike because demand for cars has been relatively weak since the expiry at the end of September of a year-long car buying incentive scheme.
Many companies had previously scheduled short-time working for several days in the last quarter of the year to reduce inventories, and they have leeway to make up lost production.

French car companies' market shares have also been underpinned by favourable currency movements in important markets, including a recent strengthening of the Italian lira and British pound against the franc. Those currencies' weakness relative to the franc weighed on the French car companies' earnings last year.
-- Christine Tierney, Paris Newsroom, +33 1 4221 5452
